screens.title: Inner Classes: Nested Structures for Encapsulation and Organization
screens.subtitle: Why you might define classes inside other classes, and how each nested form changes access and lifetime

narration.text: In this lesson we explore the four nested class forms Java gives you and why they exist. Inner classes let you group a helper type close to the class that uses it, increasing encapsulation and making intent explicit. You will learn what makes a member inner class different from a local or anonymous one, and how a static nested class behaves like a top-level type but remains grouped for clarity. We’ll look at syntax, how to instantiate each form, and the practical trade-offs: access to private members, scoping rules for local variables, and the risk of implicit outer references that can cause memory leaks. You will see concrete examples for iterators, one-off event handlers, and a static node type used in collections. By the end you should be able to pick the right nested form for a task and avoid common pitfalls like misusing outer instances or confusing static access rules. Consider how grouping a small helper type inside its outer class can make code easier to read and maintain.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Nested classes let you place related functionality close to the owner type. Choose member, local, anonymous, or static based on lifetime, access needs, and clarity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Inner Classes Overview
Inner Classes
Encapsulation and organization by nesting classes where they logically belong.

Defining a class inside another creates a special relationship. Some nested types are tied to an outer instance and can access private members; some are static and act like grouped top-level types. Understanding these patterns helps you design clearer APIs and avoid subtle bugs like unexpected memory retention.

Visual Overview
Member Inner
Instance-tied helper with access to outer state.
Local Inner
Scoped to a block, uses effectively final locals.
Anonymous
One-off implementation of an interface or class.
Static Nested
No implicit outer instance; accesses static members only.
Explore Key Topics
Syntax & Instantiation
How to create each nested type
Access Rules
What each type may read or write
Use Cases
Iterators, handlers, nodes
Grouped cards show relationship
Think of nested classes as helpers kept inside a file but closer to their owner.
Example: Iterator
A member inner class can implement an iterator that reads the outer collection’s private fields directly, avoiding extra getters.
Example: One-off Handler
An anonymous inner class is ideal for a short-lived event callback where writing a named class would be verbose.
Example: Node Type
A static nested node groups the node type with a collection class while avoiding implicit outer references.
Warning
Non-static inner classes hold an outer reference that can cause memory leaks if misused.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define inner classes and explain why they help with encapsulation and readability. You will distinguish member inner classes, local inner classes, anonymous inner classes, and static nested classes by their declaration, lifecycle, and access to outer members. You will also be able to write the correct instantiation syntax for each type and use them in practical scenarios such as custom iterators, one-off event handlers, and static node types. Finally, you will understand the access rules that control which outer members a nested type can read or modify, and you will recognize common mistakes like implicit outer references that can prevent garbage collection. These skills matter because they let you keep helper types close to the code that uses them, reduce unnecessary public APIs, and avoid subtle runtime problems. You will also create a static nested class suitable for a node or entry type that does not require an outer instance. screens.title: What is an Inner (Nested) Class?
screens.subtitle: A clear definition with reasons to use nesting

narration.text: An inner or nested class is simply a class defined inside another class. This definition may sound small, but the implications matter: nested classes create a tight logical grouping, letting a helper type sit next to the code it complements instead of being a separate top-level file. They provide stronger encapsulation because you can keep helper types package-private or private and still access outer members when instance-tied. The primary motivations are readability, logical grouping, and maintaining a focused A P I surface. For example, a linked list can carry its node class as a static nested type so users only see the collection A P I while the node type remains an implementation detail. A member inner iterator can be private and still manipulate the outer’s private fields without exposing those fields. A common misconception is that nesting always means a performance penalty; while an implicit outer reference exists for non-static inner classes, that cost is about object references and can be avoided by choosing a static nested class when appropriate. Consider whether a type truly benefits from being colocated with its owner before nesting it.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: Nested classes group related types; choose nesting to improve encapsulation and reduce public API clutter.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Definition
Inner class — the concept
A class declared inside another class to group related functionality and control visibility.

Reasons to use nested classes include tighter encapsulation, keeping implementation details out of the public API, and making intent clearer by colocating a helper type with its owner. They also can access outer class members, which is convenient for helper objects like iterators.

  • Encapsulation: keep helper logic hidden.
  • Readability: related types are nearby.
  • Access: instance nested types can read private outer members.
Key Takeaway

Nesting is a design choice to improve encapsulation and maintainability; avoid nesting when it reduces clarity.

Analogy
Think of the outer class as a toolbox and the nested class as a specialized tool stored inside. If the tool is only useful for that toolbox, keep it inside; if it’s general-purpose, make it separate.
Concrete example
A linked list class commonly groups a Node as a nested static type so node structure stays internal while the list API remains clean for users.
When to nest: Helper types used only by the outer class.
When to avoid: When nesting hides a reusable type that other packages should use.

screens.title: Member Inner Classes
screens.subtitle: Instance-tied helpers that access outer instance members

narration.text: A member inner class is declared inside an outer class without the static keyword. The important property is that each member inner instance is associated with a specific outer instance. That association gives the inner class direct access to the outer instance's fields and methods, including private ones. This makes member inner classes useful for helpers like iterators that need to inspect or mutate private state on the outer object. Instantiation requires an outer instance first; for example, you create the outer object and then call outer. new InnerType to obtain a member inner object. A common misconception is that member inner classes are always anonymous or short-lived; they can be long-lived objects, and in those cases you must be careful because the inner object implicitly keeps a reference to the outer object. This can prevent the outer object from being garbage collected if the inner object escapes the intended scope. A practical example is a custom iterator where the iterator accesses private collection fields directly. The correct choice between member inner and static nested often depends on whether the nested type needs access to the outer instance.

keyIdea.title: Member inner core
keyIdea.text: Member inner classes are bound to an outer instance and can access its private members; instantiate using outerRef.new Inner().

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Member Inner Class
Core properties
  • Declared as a non-static class inside another class.
  • Instance of inner class requires an outer instance.
  • Has direct access to outer's fields and methods, including private ones.
Instantiation pattern
Use the outer instance to create the inner: Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
Key Takeaway

Member inner classes are ideal when a helper must share the outer instance state, but be mindful of lifecycle and memory references.

Example — iterator helper
class Outer {
  private String outerMessage = "Hello from Outer!";
  class Inner { // Member Inner Class
    public void display() {
      System.out.println(outerMessage); // Accesses private outer member
    }
  }
}
// Instantiate:
// Outer outer = new Outer();
// Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
// inner.display();
Misconception: Member inner classes always need to be private. They can be public or protected depending on your API design, but prefer limiting visibility to the minimal required scope.

screens.title: Local Inner Classes
screens.subtitle: Types declared inside a method, bound to the block scope

narration.text: A local inner class is defined inside a method, constructor, or any block. Its visibility is limited to that block, making it an excellent choice when you need a class only within a single method. Local inner classes cannot be static and they can access local variables only if those variables are final or effectively final — meaning the variable is assigned once and not modified thereafter. This allows the local class to safely capture values from the surrounding scope. A practical example is a calculation method that builds a helper type to perform several steps, then instantiates it and calls a method. Local inner classes keep this helper code out of the outer type’s broader A P I while letting you organize complex method logic into a small type. One misconception is that a local inner class can freely modify captured local variables; it cannot. If you need mutable shared state, use a final container object or prefer member fields. Remember that the class is invisible outside its block, which is exactly the point for encapsulating method-specific logic. Local Inner Classes means local inner classes live inside a method or block and can access only final or effectively final local variables.. In practical terms, types declared inside a method, bound to the block scope. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Local inner core
keyIdea.text: Local inner classes live inside a method or block and can access only final or effectively final local variables.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Local Inner Class
Rules & scope
  • Declared inside a method, constructor, or block.
  • Scope is limited to the enclosing block.
  • Can access final or effectively final locals.
When to use
For method-specific behavior where a separate top-level class would be overkill.
Key Takeaway

Local inner classes improve organization inside complex methods, but remember the effectively final requirement for captured locals.

Concrete example
class Calculator {
  public void performOperation(int a, int b) {
    final String operationName = "Addition"; // effectively final
    class Adder { // Local Inner Class
      public int add() {
        System.out.println("Performing " + operationName);
        return a + b; // accesses effectively final locals
      }
    }
    Adder adder = new Adder();
    System.out.println("Result: " + adder.add());
  }
}
Misconception: Local inner classes change the visibility of local variables. They do not; they only capture values that are final or effectively final.

screens.title: Anonymous Inner Classes
screens.subtitle: One-off class implementations declared and instantiated together

narration.text: Anonymous inner classes are unnamed classes created at the point of declaration and instantiation. They are compact and useful when you need a single-use implementation of an interface or an abstract class. Because they have no explicit name, they cannot declare constructors, though they can call superclass constructors via the syntax that passes parameters. These classes can access final or effectively final local variables from the enclosing scope, like local inner classes. Common uses include providing a Runnable implementation or an event listener. The main benefit is reduced boilerplate: you avoid writing a separate named class for short tasks. A common misconception is to assume anonymous classes are always clearer; for complex logic they can obscure readability. If the implementation needs multiple methods or substantial code, prefer a named class. Also, anonymous classes still have an implicit enclosing instance when declared inside non-static contexts, so watch reference lifecycles if the anonymous instance escapes. For short callbacks, though, anonymous inner classes are an efficient choice. Anonymous Inner Classes means anonymous inner classes provide concise, single-use implementations for interfaces or abstract classes; avoid for complex logic.. In practical terms, one-off class implementations declared and instantiated together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Anonymous core
keyIdea.text: Anonymous inner classes provide concise, single-use implementations for interfaces or abstract classes; avoid for complex logic.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Anonymous Inner Class
What makes it anonymous?
Declared and instantiated in a single expression without a class name. Often used for short callbacks or task implementations.
Pros
  • Less boilerplate for single-use behavior.
  • Can capture effectively final locals.
Cons
  • Harder to test and reuse; not suitable for complex logic.
Example usages
Greeter englishGreeter = new Greeter() { // Anonymous Inner Class
  @Override
  public void greet() {
    System.out.println("Hello!");
  }
};

a new Thread(new Runnable() {
  @Override
  public void run() {
    System.out.println("Running in an anonymous thread.");
  }
}).start();
Misconception: Anonymous equals lambda. While lambdas cover many concise single-method cases, anonymous classes can implement multiple methods or extend classes; choose the appropriate form.

screens.title: Static Nested Classes
screens.subtitle: Grouped types without an implicit outer instance

narration.text: A static nested class uses the static keyword and behaves like a top-level class that’s logically grouped inside another class. Unlike member inner classes, static nested classes do not have an implicit reference to an outer instance, which means they cannot access non-static instance members directly. They can access static members of the outer class, and they are instantiated without an outer object: use Outer. StaticNested nested = new Outer. StaticNested(). A common use is to hold an internal structure like a Node or Entry; grouping such a type communicates that it belongs with the outer type but avoids the memory and coupling implications of an inner instance. Some developers mistakenly attempt to access instance fields from a static nested class — that causes a compile-time error. Choosing static nested classes when instance access is unnecessary reduces accidental outer retention and often simplifies reasoning about memory. Think of static nested classes as private implementation types that do not carry an outer pointer. Static Nested Classes means static nested classes have no implicit outer reference and can access only the outer class's static members; instantiate directly with new outer.staticnested().. In practical terms, grouped types without an implicit outer instance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Static nested core
keyIdea.text: Static nested classes have no implicit outer reference and can access only the outer class's static members; instantiate directly with new Outer.StaticNested().

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Static Nested Class
Characteristics
  • Declared with the static keyword inside another class.
  • No implicit association with an outer instance.
  • Can access static outer members only.
When to prefer: for implementation types like nodes or entries that do not need outer instance access and should avoid holding an outer reference.
Example
class DataStructure {
  private static String structureName = "LinkedList";
  private int instanceCount = 0; // not accessible by static nested class

  static class Node { // Static Nested Class
    String data;
    Node next;
    public Node(String data) {
      this.data = data;
      System.out.println("Node created for " + structureName);
      // cannot access instanceCount here
    }
  }
}
// Instantiate: DataStructure.Node head = new DataStructure.Node("First");
Misconception: static nested classes are less powerful. They are simply decoupled from a specific outer instance and are often the safer choice for internal types.

screens.title: Combined Example: OuterClass and StaticOuterClass
screens.subtitle: Step through a complete example that demonstrates each nested form

narration.text: Let's walk through a combined example that exercises member inner, local inner, anonymous, and static nested classes. The outer class contains a private field and a member inner class that prints that field; that shows how member inners can access private state. A method defines a local inner class that captures an effectively final parameter and prints it, demonstrating block scoping rules. Another method creates a Runnable using an anonymous inner class and starts a thread, illustrating concise one-off behavior. Separately, a static outer class declares a static nested Node that accesses a static outer field but cannot access instance fields, demonstrating the static restriction. Running the main test instantiates the outer and inner objects in the correct order, calls the local inner method, starts the anonymous runnable, then instantiates the static nested node directly. A common pitfall is incorrect instantiation syntax; the member inner requires outer. new Inner(), while static nested classes are instantiated directly via new Outer. StaticNested. Practice these forms to make the patterns feel natural. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Code Walkthrough
Source excerpt
// OuterClass.java (excerpt)
class OuterClass {
  private String outerField = "Outer data";
  public int outerNumber = 10;

  class MemberInner {
    public void displayOuterField() {
      System.out.println("MemberInner accessing outerField: " + outerField);
    }
  }

  public void useLocalInner(int value) {
    final String message = "Local message: ";
    class LocalInner { public void printInfo() { System.out.println(message + value); } }
    new LocalInner().printInfo();
  }

  public void useAnonymousInner() {
    Thread myThread = new Thread(new Runnable() { @Override public void run() { System.out.println("Running from anonymous inner class!"); } });
    myThread.start();
  }
}

// StaticOuterClass snippet
class StaticOuterClass {
  private static String staticOuterField = "Static outer data";
  static class StaticNested { public void displayStaticOuterField() { System.out.println(staticOuterField); } }
}
Key steps to run
  1. Create OuterClass outer = new OuterClass();
  2. Create member: OuterClass.MemberInner m = outer.new MemberInner(); then call displayOuterField().
  3. Call outer.useLocalInner(200) to invoke the local inner class behavior.
  4. Call outer.useAnonymousInner() and allow the thread to print its message.
  5. Create static nested: StaticOuterClass.StaticNested s = new StaticOuterClass.StaticNested(); then call displayStaticOuterField().
Common mistakes

Trying to access instance fields from a static nested class or using incorrect instantiation syntax for member inner classes will cause compile errors.

screens.title: Access Rules: Who Can See What?
screens.subtitle: Compare access capabilities across nested class types

narration.text: Understanding access rules is central to choosing the right nested type. Member inner classes are tied to an outer instance and therefore can access all instance fields and methods, including private ones. Local inner and anonymous inner classes share a related rule: they can access local variables of the enclosing block only if they are final or effectively final. This prevents mutable local capture bugs and preserves thread-safety assumptions. Static nested classes differ: they have no implicit outer reference and therefore can access only static members of the outer class. A frequent confusion arises when developers attempt to use instance fields inside a static nested class — the compiler will reject that. Another nuance is the use of the this reference: inside an inner class, this refers to the inner instance; use OuterClass. this to refer to the outer instance explicitly. Finally, watch the implicit outer reference for non-static nested types because it can keep the outer object alive longer than expected. Choosing static nested classes avoids that memory coupling when outer instance access is not needed. Access Rules: Who Can See What? means member inner: full instance access. local/anonymous: can capture final locals. static nested: static-only access; no implicit outer instance.. In practical terms, compare access capabilities across nested class types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access rules summary
keyIdea.text: Member inner: full instance access. Local/anonymous: can capture final locals. Static nested: static-only access; no implicit outer instance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Access Rules
Quick comparison
Member Inner: Access to outer instance members, including private fields.
Local Inner: Scoped to block; accesses only final or effectively final locals.
Anonymous: One-off similar to local; accesses effectively final locals as well.
Static Nested: No outer instance reference; can access only static outer members.
Code note — this references
Inside an inner class, the keyword this refers to the inner class instance. To explicitly reference the outer instance, use OuterClass.this. That notation clarifies which object you mean and avoids ambiguity when both inner and outer define the same method names or fields.
Pitfall

Non-static nested instances implicitly hold an outer reference; if they escape, they can prevent outer object garbage collection.

screens.title: How to Instantiate Each Nested Type
screens.subtitle: Concrete instantiation patterns and common syntax errors

narration.text: Instantiation syntax varies by nested type and is a common source of compile errors. For member inner classes you must have an outer instance: create the outer object first, then call outer. new InnerType() to produce the member inner. Local inner classes are instantiated like normal classes inside their block since they are declared in the same scope. Anonymous inner classes are created inline where the new expression appears; there is no class name and no constructor declaration. Static nested classes are instantiated directly using the outer class’s name as a qualifier: new Outer. StaticNested(). A frequent mistake is trying to call new Inner() from static context without an outer instance or attempting to access non-static outer fields from a static nested class. Another practical issue is visibility: if a member inner class is private, code outside the outer class cannot instantiate it even with correct syntax. Practicing the correct forms in small examples immediately reduces frustration when the compiler complains about missing symbols or incorrect context. How to Instantiate Each Nested Type means member inner: outer.new inner(); local: direct inside block; anonymous: inline new expression; static nested: new outer.staticnested().. In practical terms, concrete instantiation patterns and common syntax errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation rules
keyIdea.text: Member inner: outer.new Inner(); local: direct inside block; anonymous: inline new expression; static nested: new Outer.StaticNested().

Member inner example
Outer outer = new Outer();
Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();
inner.display();

Local inner classes are instantiated inside their block as usual, and anonymous inner classes are created where you pass a new expression for an interface or superclass implementation.
Common error

Trying to instantiate a non-static inner class without an outer instance or expecting static nested classes to access instance members will both produce compiler errors.

screens.title: When to Use Each Type
screens.subtitle: Practical examples: iterators, handlers, nodes, and encapsulation patterns

narration.text: Choosing the right nested form depends on lifecycle and access needs. Use a member inner class when the helper must access and mutate the outer instance state — custom iterators for collections are a typical example. Use a local inner class when behavior is confined to a single method and you want to keep related logic out of the outer class body. Use anonymous inner classes for concise, single-use implementations like event handlers or short-lived tasks; they reduce boilerplate but become hard to read if they grow large. Use static nested classes for implementation types such as nodes, entries, or builders that are logically related to the outer type but do not require access to an outer instance. A practical rule of thumb: if the nested type does not need an outer instance, prefer static nested to avoid unintended outer references and simplify memory reasoning. Also consider visibility: marking helper types private or package-private prevents A P I surface expansion. The correct choice improves readability and reduces bugs caused by accidental coupling. When to Use Each Type means member inner for instance-bound helpers; local for method-scoped helpers; anonymous for single-use callbacks; static nested for grouped, instance-free types.. In practical terms, practical examples: iterators, handlers, nodes, and encapsulation patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use case guide
keyIdea.text: Member inner for instance-bound helpers; local for method-scoped helpers; anonymous for single-use callbacks; static nested for grouped, instance-free types.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Use Cases & Patterns
Common patterns
Iterator helper — Member inner class reads private collection fields.
One-off callback — Anonymous inner class for Runnable or event listener.
Node/Entry — Static nested class grouped with collection type.
Method helper — Local inner class to keep method complexity manageable.
Practical checklist
  • Does the helper need outer instance access? If yes, member inner; if not, prefer static nested.
  • Is the helper only used inside one method? Consider local inner.
  • Is the behavior trivial and one-off? Anonymous inner or lambda may suffice.
Key Takeaway

Match nested type to lifetime and access need. Prefer clarity over clever nesting.

screens.title: Memory Leaks, this Reference, and Clarity
screens.subtitle: Avoiding subtle runtime and readability problems

narration.text: There are a few recurring mistakes developers make with nested classes. First, non-static inner classes implicitly hold a reference to their enclosing outer instance. If you create an inner object and let it escape — for example, store it in a long-lived collection — that inner object will keep the outer instance alive and may lead to memory retention. The remedy is to prefer static nested classes when you do not need outer instance access, or avoid leaking member inner instances beyond the intended scope. Second, the keyword this inside an inner class refers to the inner instance. To refer explicitly to the outer instance, use OuterClass. this. Misunderstanding this leads to subtle bugs when methods or fields share names across inner and outer. Third, anonymous classes are convenient but can hide substantial logic; if the implementation grows, refactor into a named nested or top-level class for readability and testability. Finally, do not assume nested equals private: visibility modifiers still apply. Balance the encapsulation benefits of nesting with readability, and prefer static nested classes when outer state access is not required.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls to avoid
keyIdea.text: Avoid leaking member inner instances and misusing this; prefer static nested types to prevent implicit outer references when not needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Mistakes & Memory
Memory leak risk
Non-static inner objects hold an implicit reference to the outer instance. If an inner object is stored in a long-lived structure, the outer instance cannot be collected even if you expect it to be eligible for garbage collection.
Avoid this

Do not let member inner instances escape unless intended. Use static nested classes when outer instance access is not required.

this vs OuterClass.this
Inside an inner class, this refers to the inner instance. Use OuterClass.this to refer to the outer instance explicitly, especially when both define similar method names or fields.
Readability tip: If your nested type becomes large or complex, extract it into a named nested or top-level class to keep the codebase maintainable and testable.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders for the four nested types and encapsulation

narration.text: Here's a short memory aid to carry forward. First: member inner classes are instance-bound helpers that can access all outer members and require instantiation via an outer instance. Second: local inner classes live inside methods and access only final or effectively final locals; they are ideal for method-scoped helpers. Third: anonymous inner classes provide quick, inline implementations for single-use callbacks or task objects but should be refactored if they grow. Fourth: static nested classes behave like top-level types but remain grouped; they have no implicit outer reference and can access only static outer members. Keep in mind the trade-offs: prefer static nested classes where possible to avoid implicit outer references, and restrict visibility to keep your A P I surface minimal. These concise rules help you pick the right nested form and avoid common compile-time and runtime mistakes.

keyIdea.title: Quick summary
keyIdea.text: Member: instance access; Local: block-scoped; Anonymous: one-off; Static nested: no outer reference.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Member Inner
Bound to an outer instance; accesses all instance members.
Local Inner
Defined in a block; can use final or effectively final locals.
Anonymous / Static
Anonymous: one-off implementations. Static nested: no outer reference; static-only access.
Memory strip

Prefer static nested classes to avoid implicit outer references when outer access isn’t needed. Use local and anonymous classes to keep short-lived logic tightly scoped.

narration.text: Keep three short reminders in mind. First, match nested type to need: instance access requires member inners, while instance-free helpers should be static nested. Second, respect scoping rules: local and anonymous inner classes can only capture final or effectively final local variables. Third, avoid leaking inner instances that keep outer objects alive; use static nested types to reduce implicit references. These concise rules will guide your practical choices when designing types and help prevent common compile-time or runtime surprises. When in doubt, prefer clarity: if nesting reduces readability, choose a named top-level class instead. keyIdea.text: Select nested forms by access needs, respect variable scoping, and avoid accidental memory retention.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Final Reminders
Match purpose
Instance access → member inner. No instance → static nested.
Respect scope
Local/anonymous capture only final or effectively final locals.
Avoid leaks
Do not let member inner instances outlive their intended outer context.
One-line summary

Use nested classes to improve encapsulation and readability, and choose the smallest scope that expresses your intent.
